textRun.content: Digital Transformation of the RFQ Process in Commercial Pump Distribution: INSEAD EMBA Final Project
Khoory’s Abu Dhabi estimation office turned 640 pump RFQs

into quotations in 2025 at measured median cycle times of 18, 39 and 88 working hours by complexity tier, of which only 2.1 to 11.4 hours is engineering work; the rest is queueing. Between 6 and 19 percent of quotations carry at least one defect, and against the branch’s €34.5 million of won pump orders the function leaks about twenty-five times its €33,000 running cost: roughly €177,000 a year to quality failures and €673,000 to unmanaged discounting.

We propose QuoteBench, a document-extraction and pricing layer that drafts every quote and routes each by confidence, so engineers review rather than retype and judgement concentrates on the inquiries that need it. No prototype exists: capability inputs are taken from published document-AI benchmarks as ranges and fed to a process simulation that had to reproduce the 2025 baseline on fifteen checks before projecting anything. In the central case, median cycle time falls to 2, 9 and 56 working hours by tier, and engineer touch time roughly halves.

Across 20,000 Monte Carlo draws at a 12 percent discount rate, five-year NPV runs from €1.5 million (P10) through €2.8 million (P50) to €4.4 million (P90), clearing the 15 percent hurdle in every draw, with median payback of about four months. The floor case also clears: with the win-rate uplift at zero, extraction at its pessimistic bound and the build 30 percent over, NPV is still about €0.3 million on discount discipline and error reduction alone. The remaining risk is not the arithmetic but the evidence under it: every capability input is simulated, and the pilot exists to test those inputs before the build is approved.

Strategically, automated quoting converts the branch’s inquiry flow into structured transaction data that neither manufacturers nor marketplaces hold, the distributor’s defensible position as the channel digitizes.
We do not recommend building the system.

We recommend approving Phase 1 only: a three-month shadow-mode pilot on one inquiry tier costing roughly €30,000 (S), opening with the feasibility audit of 25–30 historical RFQs on Khoory’s own documents, inside a total build budget of €92,000 and with pre-committed kill criteria at every gate.

The RFQ from Innovo Contracting for the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi lands at M.A.H.Y. Khoory's Abu Dhabi branch on a Thursday evening around 16:30: roughly 75 pumps across five applications, from booster sets to chilled water, with the quote due the following Tuesday. Khoory is competing against Grundfos, Xylem, Wilo and Lowara, and against at least one other distributor quoting the same Grundfos range it carries, so the job will be won or lost on price and speed of response as much as on brand.

Worked properly, with every schedule and specification read, head losses calculated for each application, and every selection run through the manufacturer software, an inquiry this size is close to twenty-eight hours of estimating work, and the branch has two estimators. Line managers bring both in over the weekend on overtime and borrow a third from another desk. It is not enough. Tuesday comes and the quotation is not ready.

The quote goes out two days late, seven calendar days after receipt. Innovo's senior management escalates to Khoory's leadership, and a face-to-face meeting is needed to settle the relationship. Khoory ultimately wins the project, but not on the strength of this quotation. The paper returns to what that near-failure cost and why it keeps happening.

A distributor exists in this chain because the manufacturer cannot do what the distributor does, whether economically or at all. The first and costliest of the distributor's functions is technical expertise. Every RFQ means reading consultant specifications, CAD files and drawings, extracting flow, head and efficiency requirements, running head-loss calculations, and working out which model across a manufacturer's full range actually fits the site; for unusual applications it means going back to the manufacturer for a special quote before pricing the contractor. A multinational manufacturer selling into dozens of regions cannot build that regional depth itself. It is exactly this function that nearly failed under pressure in the Innovo inquiry.

The second function is credit: rather than extend project-linked payment terms, bank guarantees and retentions to dozens of individual contractors, the manufacturer works through one distributor and lets it carry the market and the credit risk.
The third is local presence: testing, commissioning and warranty support from a party the contractor can actually reach when something goes wrong.

Each of these functions is under pressure from digitization, and this paper examines what happens when the most defensible of them becomes automatable. Credit and local presence are largely fixed costs of being in the market; technical expertise is not: it needs trained estimators and hours of manual work per inquiry, and it scales directly with volume and complexity. The question the paper pursues is whether the reading, the calculations and the model selection can be digitized without losing the judgment that makes them valuable.

A standard inquiry of three to twelve pumps across one or two applications takes an estimator around five and a half hours of concentrated work: reading the specification and CAD files, running head loss calculations, selecting the model, and pricing it. The largest inquiries, several dozen pumps across multiple applications (the Innovo package ran to seventy-five), demand twenty-five to thirty hours of estimating effort and require pulling multiple estimators simultaneously, against deadlines sometimes as tight as two to three days. These large inquiries arrive roughly once a month but cannot be staffed as if routine. Timing costs real business: an estimated 15% of tenders are lost specifically to late or rushed quotes (E, sales and management interviews; treated as an upper bound and triangulated in 9.3), concentrated among first-time customers with no relationship to buy patience, and fast-track projects landing while the team is already stretched.

Khoory carries 16 estimators across all branches, each handling roughly 12 RFQs a week across the company's full product range. A fully loaded estimator costs the business approximately €22,000 a year. Hiring a qualified replacement takes two to three months, and a further three to four months before they are fully productive. Estimator capacity is therefore a hard constraint rather than a soft one: it directly determines how fast the business can take on new sales and new customers, independent of demand.

Errors are not rare. Across the 2025 quotation audit, roughly one standard inquiry in nine went out containing at least one defect (a wrong model, a wrong price, or a missed specification requirement), rising to one in five on the largest, most valuable work. The full error taxonomy and its cost consequences are developed in Section 4.4.
What process architecture could automate the RFQ process while preserving quote quality, and what evidence supports its technical feasibility?
What is the projected financial impact of the proposed transformation, and how robust is that projection under uncertainty?
What are the strategic implications for the distributor’s position in the value chain, and what implementation path best manages the risks?

Slow turnaround, hard capacity constraints and error rates that erode margin and trust are all downstream of one question: whether the distributor's technical-expertise function can be automated without losing the judgment that makes it valuable. Three research questions address it: RQ1 in Sections 6 through 8, RQ2 in Section 9, and RQ3 in Sections 10 and 11.

The scope is limited to pumps, where the technical selection burden is heaviest and the case for automation strongest; valves, HVAC and Khoory's other product lines are excluded, though they are the natural extension once the pump-focused system is proven.
The UAE only, where the volume and the pain are concentrated today; GCC expansion is a near-term next step, since specifications and practices across the region closely mirror the UAE market.

The technical workflow from RFQ receipt through quote generation, plus the submittal stage once a project is won. The commercial negotiation between quote and LOI is excluded deliberately: the paper automates the distributor's technical-judgment function, not its deal-making.

No software has been built and no pilot run; the paper evaluates the investment before it is made. The analysis rests on a calibrated simulation of the current process, an audited feasibility assessment, and a financial projection under uncertainty (Sections 6–9); a live pilot is recommended, not conducted (Section 11).

Nothing in this paper has been built yet; the study is what investment appraisal calls an ex-ante evaluation. We evaluate the proposed transformation the way a board evaluates any capital request: measure the current process, design the alternative from proven components, model what it would do, and stress the assumptions until they hold or break.

One scoping point matters for every number downstream. Khoory operates 16 estimators across its UAE branches, each handling around twelve inquiries a week across all product lines. We measured a single branch, the Abu Dhabi estimation office, whose 640 pump RFQs in 2025 are the study population; every figure in the paper, including the Section 9 investment case, is single-branch, and no company-wide scaling is used. We chose to measure one branch deeply rather than all branches thinly, because the Section 8 simulation needs step-level timings that only direct observation can supply.

Seven sources of evidence carry the paper and no other data enters the analysis: the 2025 RFQ log, three weeks of direct observation, the 120-quotation defect audit, internal and contractor interviews, the planned feasibility audit and the simulation models. Three limits of method are stated here and treated fully in Section 12: the baseline is one branch of one distributor over one year, with 22 deeply observed inquiries; the future state is simulated and audited, not observed, which is what the Section 11 pilot exists to fix; and the demand-side evidence on what speed is worth rests on history and stated preferences, which is why the financial model floors that benefit at zero.

Three sources anchor this section: the 2025 inquiry log (640 pump RFQs, M); three weeks of direct observation in which we timestamped 22 inquiries from arrival to quotation (M); and the finance ledger of credit notes and rework traceable to quotation defects (M). Figures that could not be read directly from records were estimated from sampled data or structured interviews and are tagged (E). Everything the later sections project is anchored to what this section can demonstrate.
4.1 The as-is process: a swimlane view

An inquiry arrives as an email carrying some combination of a specification extract, a pump schedule (often a scanned image), a riser diagram, and occasionally a CAD file. From there it passes through nine steps and five roles before a quotation goes back out. Exhibit 4.1 maps the path, annotating each step with touch time (someone actively working on the inquiry) and queue time (the inquiry waiting its turn).

Exhibit 4.1. Median values across the 22 observed inquiries (M). The clarification loop and the management approval loop occur on a subset of inquiries; their queue times are medians within that subset.

The exhibit carries the central finding of the current-state study: the median case consumed 5.5 hours of actual work spread over roughly 39 working hours of elapsed time (M). Six hours out of every seven, nobody was working on the inquiry at all: it was waiting to be assigned, waiting in an estimator's personal queue, waiting on the contractor's answer, waiting for a discount approval. The work is not slow; the waiting is.
Exhibit 4.2. Touch and queue medians by inquiry tier (tiers defined in 4.2). The queue share is remarkably stable, between 86% and 88%, regardless of complexity (M).

Three steps account for most of the queueing: assignment (a median 14 working hours before an estimator picks the inquiry up), the clarification loop (a median 41 working hours for the contractor's answer, during which the process cannot move), and pricing approval. Each is a handover between people, and each handover is a queue. The cost side is simpler: at a fully loaded €12 per hour (€22,000 a year over roughly 1,840 productive hours; E, payroll records), the median inquiry carries about €66 of direct labour, developed by tier in 4.3.

A single replacement circulator and a three-building museum package have nothing in common except the mailbox they arrive in, so we classified every 2025 inquiry retrospectively into three tiers by pump count, data completeness at receipt, and project value. Two staff members classified independently, agreeing on 91% of inquiries (E). The taxonomy carries through the paper: Section 7 routes by it, Section 8 samples by it, and Section 9 builds its benefits by it.
The tiers are defined by pump count, data completeness at receipt and value band; the full criteria and 2025 mix are Table 4.1 (Appendix K). The inversion in that mix is what matters: Tier 3 supplies

one inquiry in eight but nearly half the quoted value, so the commercially decisive inquiries are exactly where the process is slowest, the documents messiest, and the expertise thinnest: two estimators can handle a chilled-water package unassisted, and one of them handles most. A redesign that only worked for simple inquiries would automate the 12% of value that least needs help.
Table 4.2 consolidates the baseline. Every subsequent claim of improvement in this paper is a claim against one of these cells.

Table 4.2. Baseline metrics by tier, 2025. Cost per quote combines touch hours at loaded rates with a per-inquiry allocation of estimation software licences; defect rates were estimated by auditing a stratified sample of 120 quotations against source documents. Gross margins restate the measured tier pattern to the branch’s stated 24 percent average on revenue (D19).

Three readings follow. First, cycle time grows faster than touch time as complexity rises (an 88-hour Tier 3 median contains only 11.4 hours of work), so the delay problem is structural, not a matter of effort. Second, the defect rate triples between Tier 1 and Tier 3, tracking the volume of manual transcription each tier demands. Third, and read together with the value shares of 4.2: the business earns its margin where its process performs worst. That tension is what the Innovo inquiry in 4.5 makes concrete.
4.4 Error taxonomy and the cost of poor quality

The audit of 120 sampled quotations, cross-checked against the credit-note ledger, surfaced four distinct classes of error; the full taxonomy with frequencies and unit costs is Table 4.3 (Appendix K). Extraction errors are the most frequent (41% of defects, on 9% of inquiries), selection errors the most expensive (about €11,300 each), and calculation errors carry the site-failure tail beyond €35,000 (E). The classes differ not only in frequency but in when they are discovered, and discovery timing drives cost far more than the mistake itself: an extraction error caught at internal review costs an hour of rework, while the same error caught at commissioning costs a return shipment, a site visit, and a measure of trust.

Summed across the year, the traceable cost of the four classes comes to roughly €177,000, about 0.5% of revenue (E). Unit costs are stated at the branch’s actual 2025 order values: the audit’s original estimates were made against order sizes about six times smaller than the revenue reconciliation later established, and a defect on a larger order costs proportionally more (D19).
The chain matters as much as the total: nearly every calculation and selection error began life as an extraction problem, so attacking the point of entry starves much of the downstream taxonomy.

The larger leak never appears in an error report, because each instance looks like a reasonable commercial decision. Discounts are set case by case with no reference point in front of the pricer: matched 2025 quotations show discounts on comparable Tier 2 work ranging from 4% to 18% (M), not because the jobs differed but because the days did. Against the median like-for-like discount, the foregone margin is roughly 1.9% of revenue annually (E, about €673,000), nearly four times all four error classes combined, and invisible precisely because no single decision was wrong. Together, quality cost and discount leakage run to about 2.5% of revenue, roughly €850,000 a year, the figure the pricing engine of Section 7.6 is designed against.
4.5 The Innovo inquiry: Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, as-is

The numbers above describe the process in aggregate; the Innovo inquiry that opened this paper shows what they feel like from inside. By the criteria of 4.2 it was a large Tier 3 inquiry: a specification extract running to dozens of pages, schedules scanned as images, and riser diagrams across several buildings. Table 4.4 (Appendix K) reconstructs its path step by step, timestamped from the mailbox records and the estimators' logs: received Thursday evening and unread overnight, first touched late Friday morning, the consolidated clarification not sent until Saturday afternoon, and the contractor's Tuesday reply then sitting unread in the same shared mailbox that delayed the start.

Seven calendar days from receipt to quotation; twenty-eight hours of work across three estimators and a weekend of overtime, well above the Tier 3 median of Table 4.2. What made it memorable was not that it was unusual, but that the process could not absorb a job this size inside the deadline, however many people were thrown at it.

It also nearly went wrong, twice. A static head read from the wrong drawing would have undersized the booster set for the taller building; it was caught only because an odd duty point prompted a second look. The contractor's reply also sat unread for a stretch, because nothing in the process flags a waiting inquiry when its answer arrives. The quotation was late, and it nearly went out wrong, on a marquee project.

Contractor interviews are in progress at the time of writing (protocol in Appendix D): four to six structured conversations covering what drives supplier choice, how speed weighs against price, and, because no live system exists to observe, each contractor's stated reaction to the hypothetical of an automated quote. Preliminary conversations consistently point to response speed and error-free technical submittals as decisive selection factors, which supports the direction of this design; verbatim quotations, including any dissenting views, will be incorporated once transcripts are complete (E, provisional). Stated preferences are the paper's only demand-side evidence, and Section 9.3 treats them accordingly: as an upper bound to be triangulated, not a measurement.

Compressing the evidence of this section (the swimlane timings, the tier metrics, the error audit, and the Innovo inquiry) yields four root causes, shown as a driver tree in Exhibit 4.3. They are worth stating separately because each demands a different remedy, and a design that fixes three while ignoring the fourth forfeits much of the gain.
Exhibit 4.3. Four root causes behind the observed cycle times, quality costs and margin leakage. Each maps to a specific element of the proposed design in Section 7.

Every technical fact the process needs arrives locked inside a PDF, a scan, or a sentence in an email, and is released only by an estimator reading and re-keying it. This is where 1.5 hours of every Tier 2 inquiry goes, and where 41% of defects begin. The Innovo near-miss was this cause in miniature.

One estimator owns an inquiry end to end, so work waits for a person rather than a task, and the scarcest expertise, held by two people for chilled water, sets the pace for the most valuable inquiries. The 86–88% queue share in Exhibit 4.2 is the signature of serial ownership, not of slow work.

Gaps in the data are discovered mid-process, one at a time, each triggering a round trip to the contractor at a median cost of 41 working hours; nothing alerts anyone when the answer lands. Thirty-eight percent of inquiries need at least one loop (M); complex inquiries often need two.

Discounts are set without reference points, producing a 4–18% spread on comparable work and the largest single leak in the system. Unlike the other three causes, this one costs nothing in time, only money, quietly, on jobs that were won.

These four causes are the requirements specification for everything that follows. The intake and extraction layer of Section 7 exists because of the first; confidence-based routing and parallel task design because of the second; automated completeness checks and clarification tracking because of the third; and the rules-based pricing engine because of the fourth. The measured current state is the design brief.

This paper draws on four bodies of work. A source appears here only because a later section leans on it; the aim is to establish what is already known so the paper's contribution stands on settled ground.
5.1 Digitization of B2B distribution and the disintermediation debate

The oldest question this paper raises is whether digitizing a distributor's core function hastens the distributor's own removal. Early electronic-commerce research answered yes: online markets cut transaction costs and let manufacturers deal directly with buyers (Benjamin & Wigand, 1995). The counter-position followed immediately: intermediaries do more than pass product, and new electronic intermediaries appear even as old ones dissolve (Sarkar et al., 1995). Chircu and Kauffman (2000) reconciled the two as a cycle of intermediation–disintermediation–reintermediation: displaced incumbents can re-enter by absorbing the technology into the functions that made them valuable, provided they move before a substitute occupies the position. Two decades of wholesale-distribution practice broadly confirms the pattern: distribution consolidated and digitized rather than disappeared, with the gains accruing to distributors that made their differentiating capability digital first.

The relevance is direct: this study proposes to digitize the first of the three pillars identified in Section 2, and the IDR framing turns that from an efficiency question into the strategic one Section 10 resolves: whether automating technical expertise makes the distributor the platform of record for its market, or merely writes the manual for its own replacement. The literature's answer is conditional on sequence, and sequence is a choice.
5.2 CPQ systems and their limits for engineered-to-spec product

Configure-price-quote software is the commercial category closest to this paper's proposal: where a product family can be described by enumerable options and compatibility rules, a configurator reliably replaces expert intervention in the sales process (Forza & Salvador, 2002, 2007), offering guided configuration, rule-based pricing and automated quote assembly on top of structured inputs.

The qualifier carries the weight: structured inputs. CPQ assumes the seller already knows, in machine-readable form, what the customer needs; engineered-to-order environments violate that at both ends, with requirements arriving as drawings and specifications rather than option selections, and the mapping to product running through engineering calculation rather than compatibility rules (Hicks et al., 2000). A pump distributor's RFQ is a textbook instance. That is why Section 6 treats CPQ as a component of the proposed design (the right machinery for pricing discipline and quote assembly) rather than as an alternative to it: what the category has never solved, and what this design must, is the unstructured front door.
5.3 AI document understanding: what the benchmarks do and do not promise

Because this study fields no prototype, published evidence on machine reading of business documents is load-bearing: it supplies the priors that 8.1 maps onto the distributor's own document mix, and it must be reported with both its flattering and its unflattering sides. The flattering side is genuine: layout-aware and vision-language models have pushed the standard document-understanding benchmarks to levels out of reach five years ago, with the strongest pipelines answering well above 90% of items on the principal document-QA benchmark (Jaume et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2022; Mathew et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2020).

The unflattering side matters more here. Benchmark corpora are dominated by curated, single-genre documents, while recent enterprise-extraction evaluations show accuracy degrading sharply as schemas widen and documents lengthen: models produce validly structured output whose values are wrong. The distributor's reality sits at the hard end of that spectrum: multi-column schedules scanned as images, specification extracts running to dozens of pages, units and symbols that differ by consultant. And one piece of arithmetic reframes even optimistic per-field accuracy: at 95% per field, a twelve-field schema is fully correct only about 54% of the time (0.95¹²). That arithmetic, not distrust of the models, is why the Section 7 design carries per-field confidence scores, validation gates and human review as structural features rather than as caution, and why the 8.1 audit exists: to establish where on the published spectrum this distributor's documents actually fall.

Four decades of human-factors research warns that the failure mode of partial automation is rarely the machine's error alone; it is the human's changed relationship to the task. Operators over-rely on automation that is usually right and abandon automation that has embarrassed them, in neither case calibrating to its actual reliability (Parasuraman & Riley, 1997). Automation bias, the acceptance of a machine's suggestion in place of one's own vigilance, produces measurable errors even among trained professionals (Goddard et al., 2012), and strengthens when the human feels less accountable for the outcome (Skitka et al., 1999). The design response is to set the level of automation per function, deliberately (Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens, 2000).

The routing design of 7.7 applies these findings directly: confidence is displayed so trust has something to calibrate against; uncertain fields arrive flagged, forcing engagement where it is needed; release is an explicit act with a name attached; and the automation level is set per tier and per function. The literature's uncomfortable implication is retained rather than argued away: a reviewer who approves ninety-nine good drafts is primed to approve the hundredth, and the value-gated release rules and override logging of 7.7 are the design's admission of it.

Five options span the realistic range, from adding headcount to building everything. Each is described on its own terms and scored in 6.2; two of the rejected options survive inside the proposed design as components.

The baseline competitor is not technology at all: keep the process of Section 4 and add one or two estimators as volume grows. Its virtues are real: lowest cost, fastest to value, no implementation risk, no change management. Its limits are the arithmetic of 2.2: a qualified estimator costs about €22,000 a year (E), takes two to three months to hire and another three to four to reach full productivity, and adds capacity only in permanent, indivisible steps. Cycle time, error rates and the discount spread stay where Section 4 measured them, because the process itself is unchanged.

Grundfos, Wilo, KSB and Xylem all publish selection software: the estimator enters a computed duty point and picks from the returned range instead of reading curves off the page. This is how most distributors, Khoory included, already work, so its gains are banked in the Section 4 baseline: the tools remove roughly 20 to 30 percent of manual effort at the selection step (E, estimator interviews) and make that step more reliable. They cannot reach intake, extraction, calculation or clarification, where the delay and most of the defects live, and each tool ranks only its publisher's range.

Configure-price-quote software automates the commercial tail: line-item assembly, pricing rules, discount approvals, document generation. As 5.2 established, the category assumes structured inputs and therefore solves the wrong end of this problem: it cannot read a specification, run a head-loss calculation or select a pump, and it addresses only around 10 to 15 percent of the touch time measured in Section 4 (E), at enterprise licence prices. It is rejected as an alternative and retained as a component: the pricing discipline it embodies reappears as the rules-based engine of 7.6.
Option D: full custom AI platform.

Building everything in-house (bespoke extraction models, proprietary hydraulic and selection engines, CAD interpretation from day one) carries the highest capability ceiling and the highest exposure. It duplicates assets the manufacturers already maintain (curve data, selection logic), requires specialist engineering talent the business does not employ, and stakes the schedule on the hardest problems first, against the 5.3 evidence that extraction degrades exactly where this design would need it most. Nothing in the Section 4 baseline requires the ceiling; everything in Section 9 punishes the cost.

QuoteBench assembles proven components under Khoory's own orchestration: foundation-model extraction bought as a commodity, a deterministic in-house calculation engine, the manufacturer selection APIs of Option B repurposed as services, the pricing discipline of Option C rebuilt as rules on Khoory's own data, and confidence-routed human review over all of it (Section 7). Nothing unproven is invented; the claim is in the assembly and the routing. It is the only option that attacks all four root causes of 4.7 at once, and the only one that accumulates a compounding asset while it works: the transaction data of Section 10.

Table 6.1 scores the five options against the six criteria the investment decision turns on, ordinally, from 1 (worst) to 5 (best). The criteria are not equally weighted, and the scores are argued rather than averaged.

Table 6.1. Option scoring, 1 (worst) to 5 (best); criteria are not equally weighted. Cost and implementation risk score five-year exposure; strategic optionality scores the transaction-data asset of Section 10.

Option A wins where a conservative reader looks first: it is the cheapest and the least likely to fail, and the matrix says so. What it cannot do is move the operational needles of cycle time, error rate and discount spread, because it adds hands to an unchanged process. D and E dominate the impact criteria and separate on cost and risk: D pays a premium to rebuild what can be bought or borrowed, while E's buy-partner-build sourcing (Table 7.1, Appendix K) confines custom work to thin, auditable layers. B and C score as what they are: useful components mistaken for solutions when deployed alone. The decision therefore reduces to A versus E: certainty and linearity against operational transformation carrying genuine implementation risk. Section 9 prices that trade; 6.3 states the conditions under which A wins it.

The rejected options do some things better. Option A is faster to first value than anything proposed here (an estimator hired in March is quoting by summer, while Phase 1 of Section 11 is still running in shadow), and hiring is reversible in a way build spend is not. On touch time alone, hiring even wins the arithmetic: at the measured tier mix the average inquiry carries about 4.3 touch hours (M, Table 4.2), roughly €52 of labour at the loaded rate, so at 640 RFQs a year the labour the automation could redeploy (about €17,000 a year) does not cover the system's amortized build cost (€92,000, one internal engineer-year) and its running costs (developed in 9.4). What decides the comparison is what hiring cannot buy at any volume: the roughly €850,000 annual leak of 4.4 sits in error content and discount variance, and adding hands to an unchanged process recovers none of it (9.2). The commitment is conditional in both directions: if the 8.1 audit returns automation rates materially below its central range, or the pilot of 11.1 breaches its kill criteria, Option A is not this paper's fallback but its recommendation.
Section 7: Proposed To-Be Process & Solution Architecture

Everything in this section is a proposal: to-be times and behaviours are projections, each tagged with the Appendix A assumption that supplies its value, while figures carried over from Section 4 remain measured. Exhibits 7.1–7.3 are in Appendix B; the RFQ schema table is in Appendix G.
The proposed system, referred to hereafter as QuoteBench, is governed
by five constraints, written as obligations rather than aspirations.

First, automate extraction and calculation, and augment judgement: the system takes over the reading, transcription and arithmetic where Section 4.4 located 41% of defects, and presents judgement calls to a person. Second, no quote leaves below defined confidence without human review; in Phase 1 the gate is absolute. Third, every automated decision is auditable: each extracted field, calculation input, ranked option and price logged with source, confidence and timestamp, feeding the liability analysis of 11.3. Fourth, graceful degradation: on any failure, the inquiry drops into the Section 4 manual process with partial work attached. Fifth, every human correction is captured as labelled training data, the constraint that turns review burden into the flywheel of 7.7.
7.2 The to-be process: a projected swimlane

Exhibit 7.1 (Appendix B) mirrors the as-is map lane for lane, with one addition: a System lane into which six of the nine steps migrate, running in minutes. The queues are not compressed but removed: a runtime has no inbox. What remains of elapsed time is one internal queue (the engineer's next free review slot, a projected 2.5-hour median [A6]) and one external wait (the contractor's reply, carried over unchanged from measurement). A projected Tier 2 inquiry would need roughly 25 minutes of human attention against the measured 5.5 hours, the difference redeployed rather than removed (9.2, 11.2).

Within minutes of arrival the intake layer classifies the inquiry into the 4.2 taxonomy [A1] and validates completeness against the 7.4 schema, producing a definitive list of gaps while the inquiry is minutes old. Missing fields trigger one consolidated clarification covering every gap at once [A3], where the as-is process finds gaps serially, at a median 41-hour round trip each, and only after roughly 22 working hours of queueing and reading. When the reply arrives, the layer recognises the thread, merges it and resumes, closing the gap that left Innovo's answer sitting unread in a mailbox.

Extraction converts unstructured documents into one canonical record, the twelve-field-per-system RFQ schema of Appendix G, using language and vision models to read specification extracts, schedules and email text. Each field carries a confidence score, and it is these scores, not the values, that drive the routing of 7.7. One boundary is stated now: native CAD parsing is out of scope for Phase 1. Where required fields exist only in a DWG file, the inquiry routes to an engineer with every extractable field pre-filled and the CAD-dependent fields flagged, so degradation is to assisted work rather than manual, and the 8.1 audit measures how often this occurs.
7.5 The product data layer: classification, storage and retrieval

None of the above works if the system's knowledge of pumps lives inside a language model: models recall approximately, catalogues change monthly, and a quotation defensible under the audit constraint must rest on data that is exact, versioned and sourced. The design therefore separates reasoning from memory. Models read documents and orchestrate; a governed product database remembers: manufacturer data normalized into a typed hierarchy, hydraulic performance stored as curve data rather than prose, prices and lead times versioned with effective dates. The model never answers a product question from its own weights: retrieval runs structured filters first and semantic search second, and any response naming a model must carry the database key and data version it drew from, which is what keeps a quote reconstructible months later and correct the week after a price revision. The full specification of this layer (classification standard, storage architecture, retrieval tooling and ingestion pipeline) is given in Appendix J.
7.6 Calculation and decision layer: three separated engines
Between a validated schema and a draft quote sit three engines, kept separate because they carry different uncertainty. The
hydraulic engine is deterministic physics, not AI

and fitting losses by Darcy-Weisbach, cross-checked by Hazen-Williams, the same formulas the estimators apply by hand, encoded once; because this is settled engineering, the design's uncertainty lives entirely upstream in extraction, which is what the Section 8 audit measures. The
selection engine is a constrained search

: given a duty point it filters the 7.5 store, queries the manufacturer's selection API, and returns candidates ranked on efficiency, price and lead time, flagging duty points near a curve edge rather than accepting them silently [A5]; where several answers are defensible, Khoory's own history of chosen and winning selections breaks the tie, the Section 10 data asset used here as a sort order. The
pricing engine is rules, not learning

: cost-plus by family with a defined discount band and a reference price beside every discount decision, aimed at the 4–18% spread and the 1.9%-of-revenue leak of 4.4; machine-learned price optimisation is deferred to Phase 3.
The preceding layers describe what the machine would do; this one decides what it is allowed to do. The routing is stated as logic:
IF   min. field confidence ≥ C₁ AND tier = 1 AND value < €V₁ AND discount in band
THEN auto-draft quote → engineer one-click release
ELIF tier ≤ 2 AND min. field confidence ≥ C₂
THEN engineer workspace: pre-filled schema, flagged uncertainties, ranked options
ELSE full engineer workspace + senior review (Tier 3, CAD-dependent, low confidence)

The thresholds C₁, C₂ and V₁ are design parameters, not findings; setting them is the work of the pilot in 11.1. Under this routing the estimator's role moves upward, to exception-handler and advisor, owning the flagged uncertainties, the curve-edge calls and the Tier 3 work that genuinely needs judgement (11.2). Constraint five powers the correction flywheel of Exhibit 7.3 (Appendix B): corrections become labelled data, accuracy rises, routing admits more inquiries to the assisted paths, and freed capacity concentrates where margin is highest, a projected mechanism the pilot exists to observe. Error containment closes the loop: value-gated release regardless of confidence, escalation for out-of-band discounts, an immutable audit log, and a single switch back to manual. Whose signature a quote carries is taken up in 11.3.
Exhibit 7.2 (Appendix B) shows the layers assembled; Table 7.1 (Appendix K) states the sourcing decision per component.

The pattern: buy the probabilistic commodity, partner for domain logic the manufacturer maintains, build only the thin layers that encode Khoory's process and data, which is where defensibility lives.
7.9 The Innovo inquiry, to-be: a simulated walk-through
What follows is a simulated scenario: the inquiry of Section 4.5 processed under the proposed design, with step times drawn from the Section 8 assumptions. Nothing in it has happened.

Thursday, 16:40: the email lands and intake opens it within the minute: classified, valued, in band [A1]. By 16:52 extraction has populated the schema and validation has found the same gaps a human found on day two, with the riser ambiguity flagged as an explicit conflict [A2]; at 16:53 a single consolidated clarification is on its way, thirteen minutes after receipt instead of 22 working hours [A3]. The contractor's reply is the one interval no redesign controls, so it is carried over at its measured pace: the request is seen on Friday and answered Monday morning. Within minutes of the reply the system has merged the thread, re-validated, run the head-loss calculations, filtered the product store, queried the selection API, and holds a draft quote: models ranked, the booster duty point flagged near its curve edge, prices in band. It is waiting on someone, rather than someone waiting on it. At 14:00 Monday, the estimator's first free slot, the review turns on the flagged selections; the senior's confirmation is two lines, one alternate is added, the discount stays in band [A6, A7]. At 15:10 Monday the quote would go out with the estimator's name on it per 11.3, a day ahead of the deadline instead of two days late. Seven calendar days would become four; twenty-eight touch hours would become roughly fifteen (S: eleven to twenty across the 8.1 capability range): the review of a 75-pump draft rather than its manual construction; and neither near-miss of 4.5 would arise to be caught. These times are model outputs; the numbers they are compared with were measured, and closing that asymmetry is Section 8's job.

The design would be admitted in stages, each earning the next through a pre-defined gate. Phase 1 runs the pipeline in shadow, every quote human-released and scored against the estimators; Phase 1 is the pilot itself. Phase 2 opens auto-draft for Tier 1 only, gated on live extraction accuracy, override rates and zero escaped defects in shadow. Phase 3 makes assisted routing the Tier 2 default and revisits the deferred items (pricing optimization, CAD) on the strength of accumulated flywheel data. Thresholds are stated as symbols deliberately: they are parameters the pilot exists to determine, and the full roadmap with kill criteria is the subject of 11.1.
8.1 Capability evidence: what the automation could plausibly do

No system has been built, so nothing in this section is a measurement of a live tool; every capability figure is a simulation input, tagged S and registered in Appendix A. What we could ground, we did. The mix of document quality that arrives at the desk (clean digital PDFs, scanned schedules, email fragments, CAD-dependent inquiries) is estimated by tier from the 640-inquiry log and the 22 inquiries we observed end to end. The extraction performance the design could plausibly achieve on each document class is taken from the published benchmark ranges reviewed in 5.3 and carried as three variants (pessimistic, central, optimistic) rather than a single point. Engineer skill and inquiry complexity then spread those figures further: per-field success and confidence are drawn inquiry by inquiry, so no single accuracy number is load-bearing anywhere downstream.

We had originally designed a field-by-field feasibility audit of 25–30 historical RFQs, scored by the estimators against a written rubric, to replace these ranges with evidence from Khoory's own documents. That audit remains the right instrument, and its materials are drafted (protocol, rubric and scoring sheet in Appendix E), but it needs estimator time we could not commission for this paper. It is therefore scheduled as the first activity of the Phase 1 pilot (11.1); until it runs, the capability inputs stay on the published ranges. The consequence is stated once: if Khoory's documents score materially below the pessimistic bound, Section 9 weakens, and the pilot's first gate is built to catch it.
8.2 Process simulation: calibration first, projection second

The simulator described in 3.3 replays the branch one inquiry at a time. Before it may project anything, it must reproduce the 2025 baseline it was built from: median and P90 cycle times by tier, touch hours, cost per quote, annual volume, queue share of elapsed time and estimator utilization, fifteen checks in all, each within ten percent of the measured value. The current build passes all fifteen (Exhibit F.1, Appendix F); the gate is enforced in code, and every to-be number in this paper is locked behind it.

Calibrating taught us three things about the office that no interview surfaced: the estimators work small jobs first, which is why Tier 1 waits stay short at 68 percent utilization; assignment delay is queueing, not procedure; and clarification waiting overlaps other queues rather than adding to them. Each finding changed the model before it passed.

With the baseline earned, the Section 7 design runs under the 8.1 capability ranges. In the central case, median cycle time falls from 18 to about 2 working hours for Tier 1, from 39 to 9 for Tier 2 and from 88 to 56 for Tier 3, with P90s falling in step (Exhibit 8.2); median engineer touch drops from 2.1 to 0.8 hours, 5.5 to 2.7 and 11.4 to 6.2 by tier (S). Routing stays cautious: 15 percent of Tier 1 inquiries release as auto-drafts and a quarter go out assisted; Tier 2 is one-fifth assisted; every Tier 3 quote stays with an engineer, worked in the pre-filled workspace. Engineering hours on quoting fall from about 2,780 to about 1,380 a year at unchanged volume, and the stress runs of 9.6 show the same two estimators absorbing a 40 percent demand surge that breaks the as-is desk. Escaped defects hold at parity with the baseline (9.1 versus 9.2 percent of inquiries), which is a design constraint rather than a bonus: reviewer attention drops on machine-drafted work, and the routing thresholds are set so the two effects cancel.
Simulated cycle-time distributions by tier, as-is versus to-be central case; dashed lines mark medians (S).

The degradation requirement of 7.1 also holds: with extraction forced to zero, the model reproduces the as-is baseline, so a failed capability assumption returns the office to today's process rather than to something worse.

Validation by the people involved is partly done and partly scheduled. The estimators challenged the swimlane, the tier taxonomy and the error audit during measurement, and two of their corrections (small jobs first, clarification overlapping other waits) became load-bearing calibration facts in 8.2. The contractor interviews (protocol in Appendix D) and a structured review of the Section 7 architecture are in progress; their scores and dissents will be reported here, and the routing thresholds they challenge are the same parameters the pilot re-measures.

What the evidence supports: the measured baseline and its costs (Section 4); the calibrated capacity arithmetic of 8.2; and roughly €210,000 a year of simulated benefit that does not depend on winning a single additional order (the labour, error and discounting effects of 9.2). What remains unproven: extraction accuracy on Khoory's own documents; contractor acceptance of faster, system-assembled quotes; engineer adoption of the review workspace; and above all the win-rate response to speed, which 9.5 shows carries the investment case. Each unproven item maps to a Phase 1 pilot measurement with a go/no-go gate in 11.1, and the floor case in 9.5 states what happens if the pilot returns the pessimistic answer.
9.1 Baseline economics of the quoting function (measured)

The quoting function is cheap to run and expensive to get wrong. Direct quoting cost is about €33,000 a year: 636 inquiries at €25, €66 and €137 per quote by tier (E), absorbing about 2,780 engineer hours. The revenue those hours carry is stated, not derived: the branch's 2025 pump-only revenue was approximately AED 150 million, €34.5 million at the paper's conversion (M, management figure, D19), and the simulator's value model reproduces it with about €136 million quoted implied by the measured win rates (S), including two flagship-scale projects a year (D17). Throughput is roughly €17 million of won value per estimator per year. The leakage dwarfs the labour: quality failures cost about 0.5 percent of revenue (E, €177,000 at the restated unit costs) and unmanaged discounting another 1.9 percent (E, €673,000), so the office leaks about twenty-five times what it costs to operate.
Exhibit 9.1 shows the projected annual benefit at full adoption, central case, as four bars that do not overlap by construction: each is computed on its own base.

Engineering capacity, €17,000 a year (S): about 1,400 hours valued at the loaded rate, not at revenue. The assumption is redeployment rather than redundancy; the hours move to Tier 3 work, declined inquiries and the clarification chase, which also defuses the change-management tension addressed in 11.2.

Error cost, €20,000 a year (S): escaped-defect cost on won orders at the restated unit costs, with overall defect rates held at parity (8.2); the saving comes from the mix shifting away from expensive selection errors, not from a lower headline rate.

Discounting discipline, €174,000 a year (S): at the actual revenue base this is the anchor benefit, larger than labour and errors together by a factor of five. Quoting inside a reference band recovers part of the measured 4–18 percent spread on comparable work (M); we count only the 40–90 percent of that recovery that pricing governance is assumed to enforce.
Win-rate uplift, €779,000 a year (S): the dominant bar and the least proven, gated next in 9.3.
Projected annual benefits at full adoption, central case (S; run manifest in the public repository).

The central total is about €990,000 a year at full adoption, reached on the 7.10 ramp. A fifth benefit, volume the branch currently declines or ignores, is real but unmodelled; it is left out of every number in this paper, which is the conservative direction.

The speed–win elasticity is the single most attackable assumption, so it is triangulated and then floored. Internal evidence: sales attribute about 15 percent of lost tenders to late or rushed quotes (E), an upper bound on what speed can recover. Customer evidence: the contractor interviews of 4.6 (in progress, protocol in Appendix D) ask directly how speed weighs against price; the model takes no credit for anything they have not yet said. Industry evidence: the response-time literature reviewed in Section 5 supports a positive but modest effect. The model therefore carries the uplift as a range from zero to five percentage points of win rate with a central value of two (S); five points on a 27 percent Tier 2 base is an 18 percent relative gain, inside the ceiling the lost-tender estimate implies. The floor case of 9.5 sets it to zero outright. The stress runs add the most useful fact in the paper: the investment clears its hurdle even if speed turns out to be worth nothing at all, because the discounting and error effects carry the cost base on their own; the uplift decides how large the return is, not whether there is one (S).

Costs enter the model as ranges, and their sourcing is stated. Build: €92,000, priced as one internal software-engineer year (D10). We have no build experience of our own, so this is an analogy price rather than a vendor quotation, and the Monte Carlo carries an overrun tail to +30 percent, with 9.6 stressing to +60. Run: €15,000–27,000 a year for inference and API usage at projected volume, licences, and 0.2–0.5 FTE of maintenance; this range is provisional, and vendor quotations replace it before any build decision. Change: €10,000–30,000 once, for training and the transition productivity dip. Every range is drawn as a distribution in 9.5, and the boundaries in 9.6 state how far any of them may grow before the case dies.

The financial model runs 20,000 Monte Carlo draws over the ranges established above: extraction capability across the 8.1 variants, the win-rate uplift of 9.3 and the cost ranges of 9.4, with benefits anchored to the calibrated process model of 8.2 and phased in on the 7.10 adoption ramp. We discount at 12 percent as a WACC proxy and test approval against a 15 percent hurdle. Five-year NPV comes out at €1.5 million at P10, €2.8 million at P50 and €4.4 million at P90; every one of the 20,000 draws clears the hurdle, and median payback is about four months (S; Exhibit 9.2). At this scale the internal rate of return stops being informative (the median exceeds 300 percent against a €92,000 build); the number that matters is the floor.
Five-year NPV at 12 percent across 20,000 draws, with P10, P50 and P90 marked (S).

The floor case matters most. Set extraction to the pessimistic bound, the win uplift to zero and the build 30 percent over, and benefits still run about €180,000 a year: NPV is €342,000 at 12 percent and €304,000 at the hurdle. The project clears on cost, error and discounting alone. That reverses the burden the case carries: the question is no longer whether the economics survive a disappointing pilot, but whether the capability assumptions under them survive contact with Khoory's own documents. Every input above the measured baseline is simulated, and a result this one-sided is an argument for testing the inputs, not for skipping the test. Phase 1 measures exactly that first: extraction accuracy on Khoory's own documents and the win-rate response on live inquiries (11.1).

Exhibit 9.3 ranks the levers one at a time. The win uplift dominates: its zero-to-five-point range moves NPV by €5.3 million, thirteen times the next lever (pricing adoption, €0.4 million), with extraction capability close behind and run cost, build overrun and change cost together barely visible. The same stress runs return a finding a marginal case could not: within every tested range, no single lever kills the case at the hurdle. The uplift at zero still clears (€0.43 million at the hurdle), the build at six times plan still clears, run costs at €200,000 a year still clear, and demand at one-fifth of the 2025 rate still clears (S). The pilot's kill criteria are therefore evidential rather than financial: the 11.1 gates guard the simulated inputs (live extraction accuracy, override rates, escaped defects) rather than an NPV threshold, alongside the operating point the simulator's search proposes: auto-draft threshold 0.85, assisted threshold 0.70 and a discount band of plus or minus 1 percent (S, proposed; the pilot validates all three).
One-at-a-time sensitivity of five-year NPV at 12 percent (S).

The Innovo inquiry closes its loop here. As measured in 4.5: 28 touch hours across three estimators, about €340 of direct cost, seven calendar days, issued two days late. As simulated at the central case, applying the 8.2 Tier 3 ratios: roughly 15 touch hours (11 to 20 across the capability range), about €180, and about four calendar days, with the contractor's reply carried at its measured pace; the quote goes out a day inside the deadline (S). The €160 of processing saved is beside the point. On a package of this size the margin at stake is roughly €1.4–2.6 million (S, register arithmetic: the D19 flagship value range at the Tier 3 margin), and what the redesign buys is the deadline, plus the absence of the two near-misses that almost turned a late quote into a wrong one.

Appendix J (extract): Product Data Layer Technical Specification

Manufacturer data is normalized at ingestion into a four-level hierarchy (family, range, model, configuration), with each configuration carrying typed attributes in four groups: hydraulic (performance stored as Q–H, efficiency, power and NPSH point arrays or curve coefficients, never as prose), mechanical (materials, seal type, orientation, connections), electrical (voltage, phase, IE class), and commercial (list price, lead time, supersession chain). Attribute naming follows the ETIM classification standard where the manufacturer supplies it, with a mapping table for house conventions, so that a model designation means exactly one thing to every layer of the system, and remains comparable if further manufacturers are added later.

Two stores, chosen by data type. Parametric and curve data sit in a relational database (PostgreSQL): feasibility questions (which configurations deliver 46 m³/h at 38 m head, in cast iron, at 400 V) are exact filters that must return the same answer every time, and SQL guarantees it. Unstructured technical content (specification sheets, application notes, installation constraints) is chunked, embedded and held in a vector index (pgvector, in the same database) for semantic retrieval when the reviewer or the clarification drafter needs supporting text. Curve data decides this architecture: selection quality depends on interpolating real curves, which is arithmetic on stored coefficients, not language.

The model is granted tools (a structured query against the relational store, semantic search over the vector index, and the manufacturer's live selection API of 7.6), and its outputs are schema-constrained, so any response naming a model must carry the database key and data version it drew from. Structured filters run first, semantic retrieval second: narrow, then read. Every record carries source and effective date, and each quote references the price-list and curve versions it used. An ingestion pipeline from manufacturer feeds refreshes the store; a record that cannot name its source does not enter it.
